title: Strategy Pattern
summary: Encapsulating interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so pricing, sorting, or routing logic can vary independently of the code that calls it.

slides.markdown:
**Strategy** lets you swap the algorithm behind a behavior without touching the code that calls it. Think of a checkout page: the *place order* button never changes, but the pricing math behind it can be flat-rate, tiered, or promo-driven depending on the cart. Strategy is the pattern that makes that swap a plug-in, not an if/else ladder.

You'll reach for it anywhere "the *what*" varies but "the *when/how it's called*" doesn't — sorting, routing, pricing, compression, validation.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: an algorithm that needs to vary independently of its caller
slides.markdown:
Say a `ShoppingCart` needs to compute a total three different ways: no discount, a 10% loyalty discount, and a buy-one-get-one promo. The naive fix is a `discountType` field and an `if/elif` chain inside `calculateTotal()`.

That works until promo #4 arrives — now you're editing `ShoppingCart` itself, re-testing every existing discount to make sure you didn't break it, and the class keeps growing. The **cart's job** is holding items and totals; **pricing logic** is a separate concern that changes on its own schedule (marketing ships new promos weekly).

The underlying problem: an algorithm's *implementation* needs to vary independently of the object that *uses* it, without that object knowing every variant exists.

slides.sectionTitle: Strategy: encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind one interface
slides.markdown:
**Strategy** pulls each algorithm variant into its own class implementing a shared interface — say `PricingStrategy` with one method, `price(cart)`. `ShoppingCart` holds a reference to *a* `PricingStrategy` and calls `strategy.price(this)`, never knowing or caring which concrete class it got.

Adding a new promo means writing a new class that implements `PricingStrategy` — `ShoppingCart` doesn't change, and nothing else can break. The **context** (the cart) delegates the interchangeable part of its behavior to an object it holds by interface, not by concrete type.

This is composition doing the job conditionals used to do: behavior varies by *which object* is plugged in, not by branching inside one big method.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a context holding a swappable strategy object
slides.markdown:
A `Context` (the cart, the sorter, the router) holds a reference to a `Strategy` interface, not a concrete class. At runtime you hand it any object implementing that interface, and it calls the one shared method — `execute()`, `price()`, `sort()` — without an `if` in sight.

<<< Image: a Context class holding a reference to a Strategy interface, with three concrete strategy classes (StrategyA, StrategyB, StrategyC) implementing that interface below it, and an arrow showing the Context calling strategy.execute() >>>

Swapping strategies is just reassigning that one reference — no subclassing the context, no touching its other methods.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: swapping sort, pricing, and routing strategies at runtime
Compare: Strategy vs a big if/else or switch on type
slides.markdown:
| | Strategy pattern | if/else or switch on type |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a new variant | New class, existing code untouched | Edit the branching function, retest everything |
| Where logic lives | One class per algorithm, single responsibility | All variants crammed into one method |
| Runtime swap | Reassign one reference | Usually requires re-entering the function |
| Cost for 2 stable variants | Extra classes and indirection for little benefit | Simpler, easier to read at a glance |

**How to decide:** if the variants are stable, few, and rarely touched again, a plain conditional is fine and more readable — reach for Strategy once you're adding new variants regularly or the branching function is already sprawling.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Strategy vs State — same shape, different intent
slides.markdown:
Strategy and State are structurally the same diagram — a context holding an object behind an interface — so the confusion is fair. The difference is **intent** and **who decides**.

With **Strategy**, the *client* picks the algorithm once (or occasionally) and it stays put — you choose `AvoidTollsRoute` and it doesn't change itself. With [State](state-pattern), the *object itself* switches its current implementation as a side effect of its own behavior — an `Order` moves from `Placed` to `Shipped` because `ship()` was called, not because a client reassigned it.

**Rule of thumb:** if the object swaps its own current implementation as part of normal operation, that's State. If only the caller decides which implementation to plug in, that's Strategy.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: strategy explosion — a class per tiny variation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every tiny variation deserves its own Strategy class — that's the pattern, right?"

**Why it's wrong:** if `RushDeliveryFee` and `ExpressDeliveryFee` differ by one constant, that's not two algorithms — it's one algorithm with a parameter. Splitting it into two nearly-identical classes multiplies files, forces every caller to pick the 'right' class, and buries the one real difference (a number) inside boilerplate (a class, a constructor, an interface implementation).

**Correct model:** create a new Strategy class when the *logic* genuinely differs, not just a value. A parameterized constructor (`FlatFee(amount)`) beats a subclass per amount. Reserve Strategy for cases where the *shape* of the computation changes, not just its inputs.

slides.sectionTitle: Where Strategy replaces subclassing for behavior variation
slides.markdown:
Before Strategy became idiomatic, the same problem was often solved with inheritance: a `FastestRouteNavigator` and a `ScenicRouteNavigator`, each a subclass of `Navigator` overriding `getDirections()`. That locks the choice in at compile time — you can't switch a navigator's strategy after it's built — and every combination of behaviors needs its own subclass.

Strategy replaces that inheritance hierarchy with composition: one `Navigator` class, and a `RouteStrategy` object plugged in and swappable at runtime. This is a specific case of a broader principle — favor composing behavior from small interchangeable objects over building deep subclass hierarchies — and it's one of the clearest illustrations of why.

Interview signal: if you're asked to fix a class with a combinatorial explosion of subclasses, Strategy is usually the fix.
